scenes.title: Watch the whole story first

beats.text: Consider a wooden crate sitting on a rough floor. Nobody is pulling it. It just sits there... and there is no friction at all, because nothing is trying to slide it.
Now a rope pulls gently to the right. The crate does not move. Friction has appeared, pulling back to the left, exactly matching the pull.
Pull harder. Still no movement. Friction grows too, matching the pull again... but friction has a limit.
At the limit, the crate is on the point of moving. One more newton...
...and it slides. Now friction stays at its maximum, and the extra pull accelerates the crate.

scenes.title: Which way does friction act?

beats.text: The forces you always have: the weight, m g, downwards, and the normal reaction, R, upwards. With no sideways force, there is no friction.
Add a sideways pull, and friction appears: parallel to the surface, and opposite to the way the crate would slide.
One contrast. If the surface is smooth, friction is zero, however hard you pull. Only a rough surface gives friction.

scenes.title: The rule: f ≤ μR

beats.text: Here is the rule. The friction force is less than or equal to mu times R.
f is the friction actually acting, R is the normal reaction, and mu, the coefficient of friction, depends on the two materials touching: large for rubber on gravel, small for wet ice.
beats.caption: μ depends on the two surfaces

beats.text: The biggest friction can ever be is mu R. We call it f max. At f max the object is in limiting equilibrium: on the point of moving.
Remember: friction is only at its maximum when the object is about to move, or moving.
beats.caption: Friction is not always at its maximum

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: Now the full question. A crate of mass five kilograms rests on a rough horizontal floor.
The coefficient of friction between the crate and the floor is zero point four. Take g as ten.
A horizontal rope pulls the crate with a force X. There are three separate trials, each starting from rest: X equals twelve newtons, twenty newtons, and twenty-five newtons.
For each trial, find the friction force and the acceleration of the crate. First... what is the most friction this floor can give? Take a moment.

scenes.title: Normal reaction, then the limit

beats.text: Vertically the crate does not move, so those forces balance: R minus m g equals zero.
So R equals five times ten, which is fifty newtons.
Now the limit. f max equals mu R.
That is zero point four times fifty...
...twenty newtons. The floor can give at most twenty newtons of friction. Keep that number in view; every trial is compared with it.

scenes.title: Trial one and trial two

beats.text: Trial one. The pull is twelve newtons. Is twelve bigger than twenty? No. So the crate stays at rest, and friction matches the pull.
Horizontally, resultant force equals mass times acceleration: X minus f equals m a.
At rest, so a is zero: twelve minus f equals five times zero.
Twelve newtons of friction, acceleration zero. Friction is twelve, not twenty: it only gives what is needed.
Reset: the crate is at rest again, and now the pull is twenty newtons. That equals the limit exactly. The crate is in limiting equilibrium: still at rest, but on the point of moving.
Again at rest: twenty minus f equals five times zero.
Friction is twenty newtons, its maximum, and the acceleration is still zero.

scenes.title: Trial three: it slides

beats.text: Reset once more. The pull is twenty-five newtons. That is bigger than twenty, so the crate slides, and friction sits at its maximum, twenty newtons.
Resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
Twenty-five minus twenty equals five a.
Five equals five a, so the acceleration is one metre per second squared, to the right.
Only the pull beyond the limit accelerates the crate.

scenes.title: What would change on ice?

beats.text: What would change if the floor were icy, with mu zero point one? The limit drops to zero point one times fifty: five newtons. Now even the twelve newton pull slides the crate.
